title: Cops, ambulance crew sued over man's demise; Hospital ruled out, jail ruled in
article: The family of Ian Alexander Young, who died after being held in police custody, is suing the RCMP and the paramedics who had earlier given medical treatment to the Maple Ridge man.

On Oct. 17, 2008, paramedics were dispatched to the intersection of 115th Avenue and Waresley Street after receiving a 911 call that an individual was lying on the sidewalk with apparent head injuries.

They found Young, 55, lying face up, his legs and lower back on the sidewalk and his upper torso on the road. They determined Young did not need to be taken to hospital and asked for help from RCMP, according to a statement of claim filed in B.C. Supreme Court.
Police also determined that there was no need for Young to be hospitalized and he was taken to the drunk tank at the Ridge Meadows RCMP detachment.
Young, who had been drinking with friends, though not heavily, earlier in the evening, was left for the night in the cell.
The following day he was found unresponsive in the cell. He was taken to Royal Columbian Hospital in New Westminster but died the next day as a result of a severe brain injury, says the lawsuit.
"As a result of the negligence and/or gross negligence of the defendants and the subsequent death of Mr. Young, the plaintiffs have suffered and continue to suffer damage, loss and expense."
The plaintiffs are identified as Karen Elizabeth Young, the wife of Ian Young, and his infant daughter.

They say they have also suffered physically, psychologically and emotionally and particulars of their damages, loss and expense include funeral expenses, loss of employment income, childcare expenses and housekeeping expenses.
General, special, aggravated, exemplary and/or punitive damages are being sought.
In August, a coroner's jury recommended that more needed to be done to look after people with head injuries while they were in police custody.
Drunks who have had head trauma should be taken directly to hospital by ambulance workers, the jury found.
Coroner Vincent Stancato ruled that the death of Young was an accident.
Cause of death was determined to be a massive brain injury as a result of blunt-force trauma, with chronic alcoholism playing an underlying role.
No statement of defence has been filed. A statement of claim contains allegations that have not been proven in court.
